title: Move division off the execute critical path
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 156-cell, 199.837 ns worst path
passes through forwarding, execute, and the combinational ALU. Four inferred
32-bit division/remainder expressions leave a very deep path in execute and
consume logic even when the current instruction is a simple load or add.
CoreMark fitness is dominated by this low Fmax, so a localized multicycle
divide unit has room to improve the clock enough to repay its rare stalls.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the real-hardware DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU datapaths with one shared
radix-4 restoring divider that performs two quotient bits per clock. Latch
forwarded operands and signedness when a divide enters EX, iterate for 16
clocks, then select quotient or remainder and correct signs. Handle division
by zero and signed overflow exactly as RV32M specifies. Keep single-cycle
arithmetic and multiplication in the existing ALU. While division runs,
retain the dividing instruction in ID/EX and hold fetch, but let each older
EX/MEM instruction drain exactly once by injecting bubbles into EX/MEM; give
an outstanding dmem stall priority before starting or completing division.
Emit the result to EX/MEM once, then resume normal forwarding and retirement.
Preserve the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS substitution for shallow formal runs while
exercising the actual divider in simulation, cosim, and deep formal. Expect
the much shorter ALU path to outweigh the added divide cycles in CoreMark.

title: Replace combinational division with an iterative EX unit
motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 199.837 ns worst path crosses
forwarding, EX, and the ALU through 156 logic cells. The RV32M DIV/REM
operators currently infer a full combinational divider in that path,
while the core occupies 12,312 LUT4s. A sequential divider should shorten
the clock period and reduce LUT use enough to outweigh its extra cycles
on the comparatively infrequent divide and remainder instructions.

hypothesis.motivation:
The baseline reaches only 5.442 MHz. Its 199.837 ns worst path crosses

operators currently infer a full combinational divider in that path,
while the core occupies 12,312 LUT4s. A sequential divider should shorten
the clock period and reduce LUT use enough to outweigh its extra cycles
on the comparatively infrequent divide and remainder instructions.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational signed and unsigned division and remainder
operators with one shared 32-step restoring divider in EX. Capture forwarded
operands and the operation when an eligible DIV, DIVU, REM, or REMU starts;
compute quotient and remainder together, then send exactly one result into
EX/MEM. Preserve RISC-V divide-by-zero and signed-overflow results. During
division, hold PC and ID/EX, inject invalid bubbles into EX/MEM so older
instructions can finish, and clear MEM/WB validity after they drain. Give
an older dmem stall priority over divider launch or completion. Gate branch
redirects and memory requests by valid instruction state so a held EX
instruction cannot redirect or retire twice. Keep RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS on
its existing single-cycle algebraic path for the bounded formal checks.
Removing the combinational divider from the timed ALU path should lift Fmax
substantially with a modest CoreMark cycle penalty.

title: Predict conditional branches before execute
motivation:
The current five-stage core learns a branch outcome in EX, then flushes
the fetched instruction and the ID/EX input on every taken branch. CoreMark
repeatedly executes loop and data-dependent branches, so these bubbles
reduce iterations per cycle even when instruction memory is ready. A small
direction table can remove most recurring taken-branch bubbles with little
logic compared with the existing arithmetic critical path.

direction table can remove most recurring taken-branch bubbles with little

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry, two-bit saturating branch direction table indexed by the
fetch PC, with counters reset to weakly not taken. For a legal conditional
branch, form the B-immediate target from the fetched instruction and select
it as the next fetch PC when the table predicts taken; otherwise fetch PC+4.
Steer legal JALs to their decoded immediate target in the same fetch path.
Keep fetch sequential for any predicted target that is not word-aligned.
Carry the selected predicted next PC with the instruction into EX, compare
it against the actual next PC (including misaligned-target trap fallback),
and redirect and flush only for a valid instruction with a mismatch. Train the counter once when a
valid branch leaves EX, excluding cycles held by dmem backpressure. Preserve
redirect priority over fetch stalls and hold prediction state when fetch is
stalled. This should improve branch-heavy CoreMark IPC while adding only a
small counter array and one fetch-target adder; JALR remains EX-resolved.

title: Cut the false redirect-to-load-use timing path
motivation:
After the iterative divider improvement, the measured 28.199 ns worst path
starts at the register file and ends at an ID/EX operand flop. The vendor
report shows it passing through execute, the fetch squash mux, the load-use
comparator, and then ID/EX control. The hazard comparator reads the already
squashed IF/ID instruction, making a late branch decision appear to affect
load-use detection. A load in EX cannot also redirect, so this dependency
is unnecessary. The resulting path limits Fmax and the champion's 100.32
CoreMark fitness.

hypothesis.motivation:
After the iterative divider improvement, the measured 28.199 ns worst path
starts at the register file and ends at an ID/EX operand flop. The vendor
report shows it passing through execute, the fetch squash mux, the load-use
comparator, and then ID/EX control. The hazard comparator reads the already
squashed IF/ID instruction, making a late branch decision appear to affect
load-use detection. A load in EX cannot also redirect, so this dependency
is unnecessary. The resulting path limits Fmax and the champion's 100.32
CoreMark fitness.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Feed load-use comparisons from the raw fetched instruction fields, qualified
by imem_ready, rather than the IF/ID instruction after the redirect/flush
NOP mux. Redirect still independently kills the younger instruction, and
fetch PC still gives redirect priority. Split the ID/EX register update:
retain the existing reset and bubble behavior for control and valid, but
allow operand, immediate, PC, instruction, and index flops to capture on a
load-use bubble or redirect. Hold those payload flops only during dmem stall
or divider wait, when the current instruction must truly be retained.
Zeroed control plus valid=0 prevents any side effects from stale bubble
payload. This removes the spurious execute-to-fetch-to-hazard path from
wide operand flops without changing branch latency or bus handshakes.
The shorter critical path should exceed the 4.6 percent acceptance margin
with essentially unchanged CoreMark cycles.

title: Break the execute-to-decode branch feedback path
motivation:
The champion's 28.199 ns worst path traverses decode, execute, fetch,
hazard control, and decode again. Its combinational fetch payload becomes a
NOP on an execute-stage redirect, so branch resolution feeds instruction
selection, decoding, register-file read, and the ID/EX register in one clock.
With division already iterative, this control loop limits Fmax and therefore
CoreMark fitness. The earlier structural divider attempt addressed the old
arithmetic bottleneck but did not shorten this new path.

With division already iterative, this control loop limits Fmax and therefore

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the front end around raw instruction bits and an independent
validity/kill bit. On a taken branch or jump, redirect the PC and clear the
next ID/EX valid bit without muxing a NOP into the instruction bits feeding
the decoder and register-file addresses. Gate every downstream effect of
invalid bubbles: EX redirect, dmem requests, forwarding eligibility,
load-use detection, register writes, and retirement. Preserve dmem-stall
and divider hold priority so no in-flight instruction is replayed or lost.
Compute PC-relative branch and JAL targets in decode and register them
with the instruction, leaving execute to select the precomputed target
after the branch comparison. JALR still uses the forwarded rs1 plus
immediate in execute. This removes the redirect-to-instruction-decode arc
and the branch target adder from the EX-to-PC path, aiming to raise Fmax
while preserving the present single-retire throughput. Keep RVFI PC
sequencing, illegal traps, and bus-stall behavior exact.

title: Compact branch direction prediction on the iterative-divider core
motivation:
The current iterative-divider core reaches 45.06 MHz but still pays a
recovery bubble for each taken branch or direct jump. An earlier predictor
reduced CoreMark cycles by about 6.5%, yet that experiment retained the old
combinational divider and therefore could not improve Fmax. Applying a small
predictor to the faster core should turn that cycle reduction into fitness,
provided the already critical EX-to-fetch recovery path stays short.

predictor to the faster core should turn that cycle reduction into fitness,
provided the already critical EX-to-fetch recovery path stays short.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 64-entry, two-bit saturating direction table for legal conditional
branches, indexed by the fetch PC and initialized weakly not taken. Decode
the branch immediate and legal JAL in fetch, and steer the next fetch PC to
their word-aligned target when predicted taken; keep JALR sequential until
EX resolves it. Carry only a predicted-taken bit with each instruction.
In EX, compare predicted and resolved direction, including misaligned-target
trap fallback, and redirect to the resolved next PC only on a mismatch.
This uses a one-bit direction XOR instead of a 32-bit predicted-PC comparator
on the critical EX-to-fetch path. Feed the load-use comparator the raw fetch
instruction, since redirect and bus-stall flushes already override its
result; this removes the present EX-to-IF-flush-to-hazard feedback path.
Train each branch once when it actually advances from EX, and preserve
correct flush, bus-stall, divider-stall, and RVFI retirement behavior. The
prior predictor measured a 6.5% cycle reduction; keeping Fmax within about
2% of 45.06 MHz would clear the 4.6% acceptance threshold.

title: Remove fetch squash from register-file read addresses
motivation:
The current champion's worst Gowin path starts at a register-file flop,
passes through execute and fetch, and ends in the register file. Execute
redirect selects a NOP in the combinational IF/ID instruction before ID
uses its source fields as asynchronous register-file read addresses.
That makes a late branch decision traverse the register-file read mux in
the same clock, even though a redirected fetch is invalid and its operand
values will be discarded. Fmax limits the present 117.09 fitness score.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Drive the register-file read addresses directly from the raw imem
instruction's rs1 and rs2 fields, bypassing the redirect/imem-stall NOP
mux. Keep the squashed IF/ID instruction and the existing ID/EX
control/valid bubble handling for decoding and retirement. When a fetch
is valid, raw and IF/ID source fields are identical, so operands and
RVFI source addresses remain unchanged. When it is invalid, any raw
operand read is ignored by the cleared valid/control state. Preserve
redirect priority, load-use detection, bus-stall behavior, and the
single-channel RVFI interface. This should shorten the measured
execute-to-fetch-to-register-file path without adding pipeline cycles.

title: Forward completed loads directly from memory to execute
motivation:
The current five-stage pipeline inserts a bubble whenever an instruction
directly follows a load that writes one of its source registers. The load
value is available at the memory port during the following cycle, but the
dependent instruction waits until it reaches MEM/WB. CoreMark runs with
random instruction and data bus stalls, so eliminating this serialized
load-use cycle can raise iterations per clock without adding branch
prediction logic to the already timing-sensitive front end. The previous
structural branch-front-end attempt preserved the cycle count and reduced
Fmax; this change targets a different source of lost cycles.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a direct forwarding path from the MEM stage's fully extracted and
sign-extended load result to both EX source operands. Let a dependent
instruction enter EX immediately behind an aligned load; prioritize this
MEM-load result over the ordinary EX/MEM ALU-result and MEM/WB bypasses.
If the data bus is not ready, hold the load in EX/MEM and the dependent
instruction in ID/EX until the bus supplies the result. Suppress any
dependent branch or jump redirect while that hold is active, and permit
the held EX instruction to advance exactly once when the load completes.
On a misaligned load, disable load-result forwarding so the younger
instruction sees the architecturally unchanged register value; retain
the existing trap and memory-request suppression. Keep the current
iterative divider, raw-instruction fetch hazard comparisons, single
retirement port, and all RVFI ordering behavior. A modest reduction in
CoreMark cycles should clear the 4.6 percent fitness threshold if the
new memory-to-EX path does not lower Fmax enough to offset the saved cycles.

title: Static backward-branch prediction without a counter table
motivation:
The iterative-divider champion takes 4,491,485 cycles for ten CoreMark
iterations. A previous 64-entry direction predictor reduced that to
4,201,740 cycles, but added about 500 LUT4s and lowered Fmax from
52.592 to 48.231 MHz, so total fitness regressed. CoreMark has many
loop-closing backward branches. Predicting their direction from the
instruction's sign bit could recover much of the measured cycle benefit
without the table's storage, read mux, write logic, or routing cost.

iterations. A previous 64-entry direction predictor reduced that to
4,201,740 cycles, but added about 500 LUT4s and lowered Fmax from

loop-closing backward branches. Predicting their direction from the
instruction's sign bit could recover much of the measured cycle benefit

hypothesis.hypothesis:
In fetch, predict each legal, word-aligned backward conditional branch
taken and each legal, word-aligned JAL taken. Fetch their PC-relative
targets immediately; fetch forward branches and JALR sequentially.
Carry one predicted-taken bit with the instruction. In EX, compare it
with the resolved branch or jump direction and redirect only on a
mismatch; JALR always redirects to its resolved target. Continue to
report the actual next PC in RVFI. Keep the predictor combinational
and stateless: use the B/J immediate sign bit and opcode/funct checks,
with no saturating-counter array or training path. Share target-add
structure with the fetch PC increment where synthesis permits, and
keep the prediction bit out of the register-file operand read path.
Gate speculative steering by imemReady; give EX recovery priority over
fetch and dmem stalls, and preserve single retirement through divider
waits, load-use bubbles, and misaligned-target traps. The earlier
predictor's measured 6.5 percent cycle reduction suggests a useful
margin if this cheaper predictor retains most loop hits while keeping
the champion's Fmax nearly intact.
